method: A Hg-Cs comagnetometer mounted on a precision rotation platform measures spin precession to detect couplings between Earth's electron spins and the comagnetometer's neutron/proton spins.
result: New upper bounds on coupling constants g_A^A and g_A^V are set, improving previous limits by up to a factor of 17 for ranges from 1 km to infinity.
conclusion: The results provide the most stringent constraints on long-range axial-axial and axial-vector couplings between electron and nucleon spins, but have no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Finite Slab First Passage Statistics Of Henyey Greenstein Scattering
authors: Claude Zeller Robert Cordery
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00290v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A photon entering a plane parallel scattering slab performs a random walk and eventually escapes through one of the two faces or is absorbed. The scattering distribution is a Henyey Greenstein phase function and the step length distribution is exponential. The central result of this paper is that the reflectance, transmittance, absorptance, and emergent angular distributions can all be expressed in terms of the first passage statistics of the walk. Two approaches are used. In the Monte Carlo MC approach, an extremely long random walk with many steps is efficiently generated without regard to any boundaries. The intersection of this walk with a large collection of target objects creates an ensemble of excursions of the objects. The MC approach relies explicitly on the memoryless property of the exponential distribution so that the portion of the first and last steps inside the object follow the same length distribution as the walk steps. The details of each excursion are recorded and any statistics can be extracted, to the sampling precision, from the database of excursions. In particular, first passage statistics are extracted from this ensemble. In this work the objects are slabs with different positions and thicknesses. In the radiative transfer RT approach the slab is divided into thin layers with scattering treated to first order in each layer. The RT equations are then directly integrated over the slab to give the desired first passage statistics. In the RT approach reflection, transmission and absorption are found to the precision of the RT solver. The two methods agree to the precision of the MC over the tested range of random walk parameters.
tldr: This paper studies first passage statistics of photon scattering in a slab using Monte Carlo and radiative transfer methods.
motivation: Understanding photon transport in scattering media is important for applications like atmospheric optics and biomedical imaging.
method: Two approaches are used: a Monte Carlo method that generates long random walks and extracts excursions, and a radiative transfer method that integrates over thin layers.
result: Reflectance, transmittance, absorptance, and emergent angular distributions are expressed in terms of first passage statistics, and both methods agree within Monte Carlo precision.
conclusion: The proposed methods provide efficient ways to compute scattering statistics for Henyey-Greenstein phase functions.

title: Bridging Quantum Mechanics And Nonlinear Optics In Raman Scattering
authors: Hideaki Kano Naoki Fukutake
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00463v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a theoretical framework for spontaneous Raman scattering that fundamentally bridges quantum-mechanical and nonlinear-optical approaches. By conceptualizing spontaneous Raman scattering as a stimulated Raman gain or loss event seeded by the quantum vacuum field, we rigorously derive the spontaneous Raman cross-section directly from the third-order nonlinear susceptibility. Crucially, this framework predicts the existence of a hitherto unrecognized phenomenon: "spontaneous Raman loss" (sRL), which acts as the vacuum-seeded counterpart to stimulated Raman loss, complementing traditional spontaneous Raman scattering (spontaneous Raman gain, sRG). Furthermore, we establish a rigorous connection to the traditional Kramers-Heisenberg-Dirac (KHD) theory, revealing that the spontaneous process is governed by interference before a detector between the signal field emitted from molecules and the vacuum field itself that stimulates the molecules. This insight uncovers a direct correspondence between the sRG susceptibility and the rotating/counter-rotating interference terms in the KHD formula. Ultimately, we extend the foundational KHD theory by incorporating previously unrecognized essential terms, achieving perfect analytical agreement between the quantum mechanical and nonlinear optical descriptions of Raman scattering.
tldr: This paper bridges quantum mechanical and nonlinear optical descriptions of spontaneous Raman scattering, predicting a new phenomenon called spontaneous Raman loss.
motivation: To unify the quantum-mechanical Kramers-Heisenberg-Dirac theory with the nonlinear-optical susceptibility approach for spontaneous Raman scattering.
method: Conceptualizing spontaneous Raman scattering as a stimulated Raman gain or loss process seeded by the quantum vacuum field, and deriving the cross-section from third-order nonlinear susceptibility.
result: Prediction of spontaneous Raman loss (sRL) as a vacuum-seeded counterpart to stimulated Raman loss, and extension of KHD theory with previously unrecognized terms.
conclusion: The framework achieves perfect analytical agreement between quantum mechanical and nonlinear optical descriptions of Raman scattering.

title: Single-cell-level Distributions And Relationships Can Differentiate Cell-division And Growth Models
authors: Vikas, Rahul Marathe, Anjan Roy
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00467v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Complex interactions among regulatory molecules determine the rules underlying cell growth and division in microbial cells. While the governing molecular network may not always be obvious, it is well known that correlations among certain physiological quantities measured in experiments, such as birth-size, division-size, division-time, and division-added-size, can differentiate among various cell-division models, such as Timer, Sizer, and Adder. Here we show that, apart from these correlations, which we extend for the case of stochastic single-cell growth and stochastic asymmetric partitioning, probability distributions of these quantities and statistical relationships between them can also be used to differentiate between these division models. Interestingly, we show that these quantities can not only differentiate the division models, but also distinguish among the single-cell growth paradigms, such as linear and exponential growth. We then demonstrate this differentiability among various division and growth models by comparing our analytical results with published experimental data. We further show that these results remain valid even when the growth rate of a cell is correlated with the growth rate of cells from previous generations in the lineage.
tldr: This paper uses statistical distributions and correlations of single-cell physiological quantities to differentiate cell division and growth models.
motivation: Understanding the rules underlying cell growth and division is important, and correlations among quantities like birth-size and division-time can distinguish models such as Timer, Sizer, and Adder.
method: The authors derive analytical expressions for probability distributions and statistical relationships of single-cell growth and division quantities, and compare them with experimental data.
result: They show that these distributions and relationships can differentiate not only division models but also growth paradigms (linear vs. exponential), even when growth rates are correlated across generations.
conclusion: The proposed statistical approach provides a robust method for distinguishing cell growth and division models using single-cell data.

title: Dependency-Aware Circuit Scheduling For Multi-Core Quantum Systems To Minimize Makespan
authors: Rajeswari Suance P S, Ruchika Gupta, Maurizio Palesi, John Jose
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00469v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-core quantum computing architectures have emerged as a promising solution to the qubit scalability limitations of monolithic NISQ devices. Quantum algorithms are expressed as quantum circuits composed of single- and two-qubit gates. However, circuit scheduling in multi-core quantum systems remains largely unexplored. Reducing overall execution time (makespan), increasing core utilization, and hiding communication latency behind computation depends on effective scheduling. In this paper, we first introduce a layered scheduling approach as a baseline where quantum gates within the same layer are executed in parallel, while layers themselves are executed sequentially. We then propose a greedy scheduling strategy which schedules each gate as soon as all its dependencies and required resources are available. This allows fine-grained parallelism across cores. Our evaluation shows that on real benchmarks, greedy scheduling achieves an average 40% reduction in makespan and improvement in core utilization. The results suggest that the use of intelligent circuit scheduling to exploit parallelism can greatly enhance the speed of circuit execution in multi-core quantum architectures.
tldr: This paper proposes a greedy scheduling algorithm for multi-core quantum systems to minimize makespan.
motivation: Multi-core quantum architectures face scalability issues due to inefficient circuit scheduling, leading to long execution times and low core utilization.
method: The authors introduce a layered scheduling baseline and a greedy strategy that schedules each gate as soon as dependencies and resources are available, enabling fine-grained parallelism.
result: On real benchmarks, greedy scheduling achieves an average 40% reduction in makespan and improved core utilization compared to the baseline.
conclusion: Intelligent circuit scheduling can significantly enhance execution speed in multi-core quantum systems.

title: Generation Of Strongly Localized Skin Solitons In non-Hermitian Waveguide Arrays With The Kerr Effect
authors: Chong Hou, Boris A. Malomed, Qin Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00618v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We address two distinct nonlinear propagation problems in nonlinear optical waveguide arrays (WGAs) with non-reciprocal (non-Hermitian) couplings. First, we investigate the light propagation launched by initial excitations of two different types. The single-channel excitation creates stable solitons supported by the interplay of the Kerr nonlinearity and non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE). In this case, we derive, by means of the symbolic-regression method, an analytical formula defining the soliton existence boundary. For the broad-pulse excitation, we produce perturbed soliton solutions analytically in the continuum approximation, which is accurately corroborated by numerical results. We thus conclude that NHSE accelerates the propagation of the broad soliton towards the boundary, ultimately causing tight localization at the edge, which is a hallmark of the NHSE in the continuum limit. Second, we identify stationary solitons in the system -- specifically, nonlinear bulk modes in the Hermitian regime and near-edge skin solitons in the non-Hermitian one. The nonlinear bulk modes are compressed toward the edge of the WGA under the action of the non-reciprocality, which is the nonlinear extension of NHSE.
tldr: This paper studies nonlinear soliton propagation in non-Hermitian waveguide arrays with Kerr nonlinearity, focusing on the non-Hermitian skin effect.
motivation: To understand how non-Hermitian couplings and nonlinearity interact to produce localized solitons in optical waveguide arrays.
method: Analytical derivations using symbolic regression and continuum approximation, supported by numerical simulations.
result: Single-channel excitation yields stable skin solitons; broad-pulse excitation leads to accelerated edge localization; stationary nonlinear bulk and edge solitons are identified.
conclusion: The non-Hermitian skin effect can be extended to nonlinear systems, enabling strong edge localization of solitons.

title: Heliciton-Assisted Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity From Helical Dirac Current
authors: Fang Shen Ju Gao
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00624v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a quantized chiral-field mechanism for chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS). The corresponding quantum is a heliciton: a helical mode with phase coordinate [MATH], screw momentum [MATH], and energy [MATH]. A helical electron can absorb or emit this quantum, converting the static chiral vertex developed in our preceding work into an inelastic resonant scattering process. Using first Born scattering theory, we show that an incident two-spin-channel state generates two heliciton-assisted sidebands. Absorption converts the [MATH] channel into the [MATH] sideband, while emission converts the [MATH] channel into the [MATH] sideband. Thus the heliciton supplies both the screw momentum and energy needed to turn the handedness-conversion into a resonant spin-selective channel. The two sidebands inherit the same sampled-current overlap [MATH] from the static theory, but acquire different kinematic weights and different resonance detunings. The sideband sector reaches full spin polarization at the respective isolated heliciton resonances, with [MATH] for [MATH] and [MATH] for [MATH]. Reversing the screw handedness, [MATH], interchanges the two sideband channels and reverses the polarization. No ad hoc spin-dependent potential is introduced. The spin selectivity comes from three ingredients: helical Dirac-current texture, quantized screw-symmetric environmental motion, and resonant exchange of screw momentum and energy. This identifies CISS as a heliciton-assisted resonance mechanism that produces spin polarization in the inelastic sideband sector.
tldr: This paper proposes a heliciton-assisted resonance mechanism for chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS) in helical Dirac systems.
motivation: To explain the origin of spin selectivity in chiral molecules without introducing ad hoc spin-dependent potentials.
method: Develops a quantized chiral-field model where a helical electron absorbs or emits a heliciton (a helical mode), and uses first Born scattering theory to compute sideband spin polarizations.
result: The heliciton-assisted process produces two sidebands with opposite spin polarizations at resonance, achieving full spin polarization at isolated resonances.
conclusion: CISS is identified as a heliciton-assisted resonance mechanism that generates spin polarization in the inelastic sideband sector.

title: Decision Feedback Differential Detection For Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces
authors: Harry Leib Jiawei Qiu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00121v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work considers a Differential Reflecting Modulation (DRM) scheme for Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) not requiring channel state information (CSI). When operating over time-varying fading channels, such schemes with Conventional Differential Demodulation (CDD) receivers experience high error floors and performance degradation. To address these issues, we propose a Decision Feedback Differential Detection (DFDD) technique for DRM. We explore the application of DFDD for RIS DRM and conduct extensive Monte-Carlo simulations to analyze performance. Results demonstrate the viability of our DFDD technique across various RIS scenarios and highlight the importance of proper parameter selection to achieve good performance. The DFDD scheme is also compared with uncoded and Differential Space-Time Modulation (DSTM) coded DRM using CDD based receivers. We observe that at low SNR, the DFDD scheme performs almost as well as the DRM with CDD scheme, but worse than the DSTM coded DRM. As the SNR increases however, both CDD-detected systems encounter high error floors while the error rate of DFDD based scheme continues to improve until it reaches a relatively low error floor. It is shown that the chief merits of employing DFDD receivers in such RIS systems is the low error floors they provide over time varying fading channels, albeit at expense of a small increased complexity.
tldr: This paper proposes a decision feedback differential detection technique for reconfigurable intelligent surfaces to improve performance over time-varying fading channels without requiring channel state information.
motivation: Conventional differential demodulation for RIS-based differential reflecting modulation suffers from high error floors and performance degradation in time-varying fading channels.
method: The authors develop a decision feedback differential detection (DFDD) scheme for RIS DRM and evaluate it via Monte-Carlo simulations, comparing with CDD and DSTM-coded DRM.
result: The DFDD scheme achieves lower error floors than CDD at high SNR, though it performs worse than DSTM-coded DRM at low SNR.
conclusion: DFDD is a viable low-complexity technique for RIS systems that mitigates error floors in time-varying channels, with a small complexity increase.

title: Guesswork Under Linear Constraints: Exact Exponent For Coset Decoding
authors: Hassan Tavakoli
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00205v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish the exact exponential growth rate of the [MATH]-th moment of the constrained guesswork [MATH] -- the rank of the true noise vector within its syndrome coset of a random binary linear code under i.i.d.\ Bernoulli[MATH] noise: \( \lim_{n\to\infty} {n}\log_2\Eb\!\left[G_{}^{\rho}\right] = \rho\,h_{{1+\rho}}(p)\;+\;\rho(R-1), \, \rho>0, \) where [MATH] is the binary R\'{e}nyi entropy and [MATH] is the code rate. The exponent shifts down by exactly [MATH] relative to the unconstrained Ar{\i}kan--Merhav exponent, with each of the [MATH] parity checks contributing equally. Finite-length simulations confirm convergence from below. We further establish: (i)~a transfer theorem expressing the partition-function exponent in terms of an arbitrary weight-enumerator growth rate [MATH]; (ii)~the exact exponent for [MATH]-list (``[MATH]-th'') constrained guesswork; and (iii)~a sharp second-order refinement of order [MATH]. Beyond the binary i.i.d.\ setting, we prove a universality theorem: for any code ensemble [MATH] whose weight enumerator concentrates at rate [MATH], the guesswork exponent equals [MATH], where [MATH]. As concrete applications, we instantiate this theorem for the [MATH]-ary extension, [MATH], and for Gallager's regular LDPC ensemble, obtaining a closed-form guesswork exponent via an exact finite-length identity for the ensemble-average weight enumerator.
tldr: The paper derives the exact exponential growth rate of the constrained guesswork for coset decoding of random linear codes under i.i.d. Bernoulli noise.
motivation: Guesswork quantifies the computational effort required to identify a noise vector given its syndrome, which is relevant to decoding and security. The paper aims to extend known unconstrained results to the constrained (coset) setting.
method: The analysis uses large deviation theory and the method of types, leveraging the weight enumerator of the code ensemble to compute the moment-generating function of guesswork.
result: The exact exponent for the ρ-th moment of constrained guesswork is ρ h_{1+ρ}(p) + ρ(R-1), where h is binary Rényi entropy and R is code rate. A transfer theorem and universality result are also established.
conclusion: The constrained guesswork exponent is a simple shift of the unconstrained exponent, and the result generalizes to various code ensembles including LDPC codes.

title: Homogenization Of $\ell_2$-Adversarial Training In High-Dimensions: Exact Dynamics Under Stochastic Gradient Descent
authors: Fabrizzio Sabelli
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00207v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a framework for analyzing the learning dynamics of [MATH]-adversarial training of single-index models on Gaussian mixtures in the high-dimensional limit under streaming stochastic gradient descent (SGD). We derive deterministic equivalents for a broad class of statistics of the SGD iterates, including the adversarial risk and distance to adversarial optimality, in terms of the solution to a system of ODEs. We use them to study two idealized learning rate schedules: the Polyak stepsize and exact line search. In the case of [MATH]-adversarial least squares with a single class, we show that, unlike noiseless standard least squares, no constant learning rate guarantees monotone descent of SGD towards a minimizer of the adversarial risk. We identify anisotropic covariance and a mismatch in ridge parameters as the main sources of suboptimality of exact line search relative to the Polyak stepsize. We also introduce a stochastic differential equation (SDE), called adversarial homogenized SGD, that captures the evolution of statistics of the iterates of SGD. For [MATH]-adversarial least squares, using this SDE, we show the evolution of the risk is equivalent, up to dimension-free constants, to that of SGD on standard least squares with an adaptive learning rate and adaptive [MATH]-regularization. When the dynamics converge, the limiting adversarial risk and SGD iterate are determined by a fixed-point equation, with the limiting iterate being equivalent to the solution of a ridge regression problem whose regularization parameter is the limiting effective regularization of SGD.
tldr: This paper analyzes the dynamics of adversarial training in high-dimensional settings using stochastic gradient descent, focusing on ℓ2-adversarial attacks on Gaussian mixtures.
motivation: Understanding the learning dynamics of adversarial training is important for robustness, but the paper does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
method: The authors develop a framework using deterministic equivalents and stochastic differential equations to model SGD iterates under ℓ2-adversarial training.
result: They derive exact dynamics, show that no constant learning rate guarantees monotone descent, and identify sources of suboptimality in line search.
conclusion: The work provides insights into adversarial training dynamics but is purely in classical machine learning theory, with no relevance to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Identifying Defective Units In Infinite Periodic Arrays Of Point Sources
authors: Dinh-Liem Nguyen, Nhung H. Nguyen, Thi-Phong Nguyen
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00241v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper focuses on identifying defective units in unbounded periodic arrays of point sources using boundary data. The study is motivated by the noninvasive evaluation of large-scale periodic source systems. Unlike classical inverse source problems in free space, the key challenge here lies in the disruption of periodicity caused by defective sources in the infinite array. To address this, we employ the Floquet - Bloch transform to reformulate the original inverse source problem as a quasi-periodic inverse source problem. We first establish uniqueness theorems for both the original and the quasi-periodic formulations. Then, we develop a new numerical method for identifying defective sources. This method combines a sampling indicator function with an algebraic technique to determine not only the number of defective sources, but also their locations and intensities. Numerical experiments are presented to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
tldr: This paper develops a method to identify defective units in infinite periodic arrays of point sources using boundary data and the Floquet-Bloch transform.
motivation: Noninvasive evaluation of large-scale periodic source systems is important, but defects disrupt periodicity, making classical inverse source methods inapplicable.
method: The Floquet-Bloch transform reformulates the problem as a quasi-periodic inverse source problem; a sampling indicator function combined with an algebraic technique identifies the number, locations, and intensities of defective sources.
result: Uniqueness theorems are established for both original and quasi-periodic formulations, and numerical experiments validate the method's effectiveness.
conclusion: The proposed method successfully identifies defective units in infinite periodic arrays, offering a tool for noninvasive evaluation of such systems.

title: Slm, Llm Or Agentic Ai? Toward Intelligent UAV-Enabled Wpt Systems In Low-Altitude Economy Networks
authors: Feibo Jiang, Li Dong, Lei Mao, Kezhi Wang, Xianbin Wang, Abbas Jamalipour
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00255v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have become key enabling platforms for low-altitude economic networks, yet achieving efficient and adaptive optimization under resource-constrained and dynamic environments remains challenging. This paper investigates language models for UAV-enabled Wireless Power Transfer (WPT) systems. First, a lightweight Small Language Model (SLM)-based solution is developed using a pre-trained BERT backbone, enhanced UAV embeddings and contextual features, a geometry-aware path decoder, and ensemble inference to achieve low complexity, low latency, and high energy efficiency. Second, an Agentic AI-based framework is designed to exploit the reasoning and interactive capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). It integrates four collaborative agents-Initializer, Actor, Critic, and Reflector-to form a closed loop of generation, optimization, evaluation, and reflection for iterative UAV path and energy optimization. Finally, simulations compare the SLM-, LLM-, and Agentic AI-based approaches.
tldr: This paper applies SLM, LLM, and Agentic AI to optimize UAV path and energy in wireless power transfer systems for low-altitude economy networks.
motivation: UAV-enabled WPT systems face challenges in adaptive optimization under resource-constrained and dynamic environments.
method: Develops a lightweight SLM solution using BERT with UAV embeddings and a geometry-aware path decoder, and an Agentic AI framework with four collaborative agents for iterative optimization.
result: Simulations compare the performance of SLM-, LLM-, and Agentic AI-based approaches in terms of complexity, latency, and energy efficiency.
conclusion: The paper demonstrates that language models can enhance UAV path and energy optimization, but the work is primarily an engineering application without fundamental contributions to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Quantum Simulation Of Stokes Flow Via Schr\"odingerisation And Artificial Compressibility
authors: Shi Jin, Jiaqi Tang, Qilong Zhai, Lei Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00281v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulating incompressible Stokes flow is essential for studies in microfluidics and low-Reynolds number hydrodynamics. However, the computational cost of resolving the associated saddle-point problem grows prohibitively with the dimensionality of the problem. In this work, we present a quantum algorithm based on the Schr\"odingerisation technique for the Stokes equations, incorporating an artificial compressibility regularization. The core of our approach is the design of an explicit quantum circuit that encodes the resulting regularized system. The artificial compressibility formulation provides a unified framework for the system, which is then efficiently mapped to a quantum circuit via the Schr\"odingerisation procedure. A rigorous complexity analysis demonstrates the quantum computational advantage of our algorithms in high-dimensional settings, notably an exponential speedup in problem dimensionality. The validity and scalability of the proposed method are corroborated by numerical simulations performed on Qiskit.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum algorithm for simulating Stokes flow using Schrödingerisation and artificial compressibility, achieving exponential speedup in high dimensions.
motivation: Simulating incompressible Stokes flow is computationally expensive for high-dimensional problems, motivating the need for quantum algorithms.
method: The authors design an explicit quantum circuit based on the Schrödingerisation technique and artificial compressibility regularization to encode the Stokes equations.
result: Rigorous complexity analysis shows exponential speedup in problem dimensionality, and numerical simulations on Qiskit validate the method.
conclusion: The quantum algorithm offers a promising approach for efficient simulation of Stokes flow in high-dimensional settings.

title: Data-Adaptive Learning Of Dynamical Systems By Matching Transfer Operators And Invariant Measures
authors: Yinong Huang, Jonah Botvinick-Greenhouse, Yunan Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Trajectory-based learning of dynamical systems is often fragile in the presence of noise, chaos, or sparse observations, as small pointwise errors can rapidly amplify. We introduce a transition-statistics approach to system identification that learns dynamics by matching the induced motion of probability mass across a data-adaptive mesh. Given trajectory data, we build an unstructured partition of state space and approximate the Perron--Frobenius operator with a regularized Ulam transition matrix. We replace hard cell indicators with continuous, piecewise-smooth partition-of-unity weights, yielding a Markov matrix supporting gradient-based optimization with respect to the parameters of a learned vector field. This enables two related training objectives: matching invariant measures through the stationary eigenvectors of the transition matrices, and matching the full transition matrices to capture transport between regions of state space. Numerical experiments on Lorenz-63, Lorenz-96, and a reduced-order NOAA sea surface temperature forecasting problem show that transition-statistics matching gives more reliable long-time dynamics than pointwise trajectory matching, particularly under measurement noise and sparse sampling. The approach provides a robust operator-theoretic alternative to trajectory-level losses for learning chaotic and partially observed dynamical systems.
tldr: This paper introduces a data-adaptive method for learning dynamical systems by matching transfer operators and invariant measures, focusing on chaotic and noisy systems.
motivation: Trajectory-based learning of dynamical systems is fragile under noise, chaos, or sparse observations; a more robust approach is needed.
method: The method builds an unstructured partition of state space, approximates the Perron-Frobenius operator with a regularized Ulam transition matrix using continuous partition-of-unity weights, and optimizes parameters by matching invariant measures or full transition matrices.
result: Numerical experiments on Lorenz-63, Lorenz-96, and sea surface temperature forecasting show that transition-statistics matching yields more reliable long-time dynamics than pointwise trajectory matching, especially under noise and sparse sampling.
conclusion: The approach provides a robust operator-theoretic alternative to trajectory-level losses for learning chaotic and partially observed dynamical systems.

title: L2-L2-gain Bounds For Quadratic Output Systems
authors: Birgit Hillebrecht
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00552v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive an explicit bound for the L2-L2-gain of linear time-invariant systems whose output is a quadratic function of the state and the input. Such systems appear naturally in many areas, for example for port-Hamiltonian systems, optimal-control, and stochastic problems. In case the output is purely quadratic in the state, the bound equals the L2-norm of the bivariate transfer function evaluated along the anti-diagonal [MATH] of the [MATH] frequency domain. Further, we show how the bound can be computed by solving linear matrix equations. This result provides a practical tool for assessing and reducing quadratic-output models.
tldr: The paper derives explicit L2-L2-gain bounds for linear time-invariant systems with quadratic output, with applications to port-Hamiltonian systems and model reduction.
motivation: Quadratic output systems arise in many areas, but their input-output gain bounds were not well characterized, limiting analysis and model reduction.
method: The bound is derived using the bivariate transfer function evaluated along the anti-diagonal in the frequency domain, and computed via linear matrix equations.
result: An explicit bound for the L2-L2-gain is provided, which for purely quadratic output equals the L2-norm of the bivariate transfer function along the anti-diagonal.
conclusion: The result offers a practical tool for assessing and reducing quadratic-output models, but does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Convolutional Symmetric AutoEncoders: Enhancing Latent Stability Via Differential Geometry
authors: G. Li Causi, N. Tonicello, L. Magri, G. Rozza
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autoencoders (AEs) have emerged as powerful tools for non-linear dimensionality reduction, often surpassing traditional linear methods such as Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) in scenarios characterized by slowly decaying Kolmogorov [MATH]-widths. In the realm of Reduced-Order Modelling (ROM), these models are increasingly utilized to learn low-dimensional representations of solution manifolds associated with parametric Partial Differential Equations (PDEs). However, the high expressivity of AEs presents a challenge: although trained networks typically minimize reconstruction error, they often struggle to capture the essential properties necessary for building accurate and robust ROMs. Recent works by arXiv:2307.15288v2 and arXiv:2506.11641v1 have tackled this challenge in fully connected AEs by proposing representation-consistent architectures, which preserve some of the properties belonging to POD. This study builds upon that concept by extending representation consistency for convolutional layers. We introduce a novel class of symmetric Convolutional AutoEncoders (CAEs) designed to embody the primary properties of manifold parametrization mappings. When integrated into a ROM framework, this architecture demonstrates significantly improved predictive capabilities. Specifically, we compared the performance of the ROMs based on classical and symmetric CAEs on three one dimensional academic test cases, namely the Linear Advection, the Viscous Burger and the Kuramoto Sivashinsky equation. Numerical results demonstrate that our proposed symmetric approach consistently yields more accurate latent trajectories, lower reconstruction errors, and enhanced model robustness.
tldr: This paper proposes symmetric convolutional autoencoders for reduced-order modeling of parametric PDEs, focusing on latent stability via differential geometry.
motivation: Standard autoencoders used for nonlinear dimensionality reduction in ROM often fail to capture essential manifold properties, leading to inaccurate latent trajectories.
method: The authors extend representation-consistent architectures to convolutional layers, designing symmetric CAEs that preserve properties of manifold parametrization mappings.
result: On 1D test cases (Linear Advection, Viscous Burger, Kuramoto-Sivashinsky), the symmetric CAE-based ROM yields more accurate latent trajectories, lower reconstruction errors, and enhanced robustness.
conclusion: The proposed symmetric CAE architecture improves predictive capabilities for ROM, offering a more stable latent representation.

title: Positive And Negative Determinant Strategies In Repeated Games With Behavior-Value Inconsistency
authors: Yuan Liu, Yakun Wang, Bin Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00625v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Direct reciprocity, based on the repeated interactions, is a fundamental mechanism to promote cooperation. Zero-determinant (ZD) strategies have opened an avenue for unilateral payoff control. However, previous studies neglect internal costs provided what agents do differ from what agents think, which is crucial for decision making of intelligent agents. Motivated by this, we establish a game theoretical framework by assuming that an individual pays the internal cost if the behavior is inconsistent with the internal thought. We prove that ZD strategy does not exist if the cost via behavior-value inconsistency is present. Instead, we find a new class of repeated strategies that enforce a unilateral payoff control, which is termed as positive/negative determinant strategy. The found strategy allows an individual to enforce an affine combination of two individuals' average payoffs above/below zero. Consequently, a focal individual is able to unilaterally control the opponent's payoff below a given value via negative determinant strategy, and a focal individual is able to get more payoff than the opponent via positive determinant strategy. We also find that the control ability of positive/negative determinant strategies is better off than that of ZD strategies. Our work highlights the importance of inconsistency between the behavior and value on payoff control, which is typically absent in classic ZD strategies.
tldr: This paper studies repeated games with behavior-value inconsistency, introducing positive/negative determinant strategies for unilateral payoff control.
motivation: Classic zero-determinant strategies in repeated games ignore internal costs when behavior differs from internal thought, which is crucial for intelligent agents.
method: The authors establish a game-theoretic framework incorporating internal costs for behavior-value inconsistency and derive conditions for unilateral payoff control.
result: Zero-determinant strategies do not exist under inconsistency; instead, positive/negative determinant strategies are found that enforce affine payoff combinations above/below zero.
conclusion: Behavior-value inconsistency significantly alters payoff control possibilities, and the new strategies outperform classic ZD strategies in control ability.

title: Recovery Of Planted Subgraphs
authors: Wasim Huleihel
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00897v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding the fundamental limits of recovering planted subgraphs in random graphs is a central challenge in high-dimensional statistics and theoretical computer science. While existing work has largely focused on special subgraph families such as cliques, bicliques, or dense blocks, the exact recovery of a general planted subgraph in Erds--R\'enyi random graphs remains poorly understood. In this paper, we study the exact recovery of an arbitrary planted subgraph [MATH] embedded in a dense Erds--R\'enyi random graph [MATH], where edges within [MATH] are present independently with probability [MATH]. Our main results identify sharp conditions under which exact recovery is possible with high probability, and we establish matching lower bounds showing the necessity of these conditions. The resulting statistical threshold is characterized by a new graph-theoretic quantity, which we term the . This quantity is defined as the maximum subgraph density of the smallest induced balanced subgraph of [MATH]. We then turn to the problem of recovery under polynomial-time constraints. We propose a computationally efficient recovery algorithm that applies to arbitrary planted subgraphs and analyze its performance in terms of certain spectral properties of the adjacency matrix. In addition, we derive computational lower bounds for recovery using the low-degree polynomial framework, establishing regimes where recovery is statistically possible but computationally hard. Finally, we consider several extensions of our setting, including recovery in semi-random models and weaker notions of recovery.
tldr: This paper studies the exact recovery of planted subgraphs in random graphs, establishing sharp statistical thresholds and computational lower bounds.
motivation: Understanding the fundamental limits of recovering planted subgraphs in random graphs is a central challenge in high-dimensional statistics and theoretical computer science, but general planted subgraphs beyond cliques or dense blocks remain poorly understood.
method: The paper derives sharp conditions for exact recovery using a new graph-theoretic quantity called maximum subgraph density of the smallest induced balanced subgraph, and proposes a computationally efficient recovery algorithm based on spectral properties of the adjacency matrix. Computational lower bounds are derived using the low-degree polynomial framework.
result: Sharp statistical thresholds for exact recovery are identified, with matching lower bounds. The algorithm's performance is analyzed, and regimes where recovery is statistically possible but computationally hard are established.
conclusion: The work provides a comprehensive characterization of the fundamental limits and algorithmic challenges for recovering arbitrary planted subgraphs in random graphs.

title: Fundamental Limits Of Random Downlink Integrated Sensing And Communication Over Rician Channels
authors: Marziyeh Soltani, Mahtab Mirmohseni, Rahim Tafazolli, Mark F. Flanagan
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00912v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies the stochastic performance of a downlink multiple-input multiple-output integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) system over Rician fading channels. Rician fading is important in line-of-sight (LoS)-dominated deployments, where a deterministic propagation component can strongly affect sensing and communication reliability. The base station (BS) simultaneously serves a user and senses a target. The BS-user channel contains LoS and non-line-of-sight components. The user LoS angle may be fixed or random, and the target angle may follow an arbitrary distribution potentially correlated with the user angle. Compared with Rayleigh fading, the deterministic LoS component introduces angle-dependent terms and leads to generally independent but non-identically distributed random vectors, requiring new analysis. We analyze two beamforming strategies: subspace joint beamforming (SJB), optimal for the shared waveform structure, and linear beamforming (LB), a practical alternative using separate sensing and communication beamformers. For both schemes, we derive communication outage probability (OP) and sensing OP based on the Cramer--Rao bound (CRB). We also identify special cases with simpler expressions. For LB, we derive upper and lower bounds on sensing OP and a tractable approximation. We characterize large-system and high-power scaling laws. LB without dirty paper coding (DPC) is interference-limited at high power due to radar self-interference. Results show the Rician K-factor affects communication more strongly than sensing, with non-monotonic behavior across regimes. LB with DPC achieves the best overall performance in strong LoS environments and is the only scheme achieving ultra-high communication reliability in Rayleigh fading, while SJB provides a robust lower-complexity alternative across operating conditions.
tldr: This paper analyzes the performance of a downlink ISAC system over Rician fading channels, deriving outage probabilities and scaling laws for two beamforming strategies.
motivation: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is a key technology for future wireless networks, but its performance under realistic Rician fading with line-of-sight components is not well understood.
method: The authors model a MIMO ISAC system with Rician fading, considering subspace joint beamforming (SJB) and linear beamforming (LB) with or without dirty paper coding. They derive communication and sensing outage probabilities based on the Cramér-Rao bound.
result: The Rician K-factor affects communication more than sensing, and LB with DPC achieves the best performance in strong LoS environments, while SJB offers a robust lower-complexity alternative.
conclusion: The work provides fundamental limits and design insights for ISAC systems in LoS-dominated deployments, highlighting trade-offs between beamforming strategies and the impact of Rician fading.

title: DRL-Based Joint Beamforming And Surface Shape Optimization For Flexible Intelligent Metasurface-Aided Isac Systems
authors: Maoyuan Wang, Qian Zhang, Jiancheng An, Xuejun Cheng, Zheng Dong, Deqiang Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00951v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) unifies high-precision sensing and wireless data transmission. In this paper, we investigate the design of ISAC systems enabled by flexible intelligent metasurface (FIM) and aim to minimize the Cram\'er-Rao bound (CRB) with quality of service (QoS) constraints using deep reinforcement learning (DRL). Specifically, we formulate the joint design of beamforming matrix and FIMs surface shape to reduce the CRB subject to transmit power, QoS and the FIMs surface shape constraints. However, the non-convex formulation makes optimization problem difficult to solve. To tackle this issue, we develop a deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG) actor critic DRL scheme for the joint design, guided by a constraint aware reward to progressively improve sensing performance. Numerical results demonstrate that jointly optimizing the beamforming matrix and the FIMs surface shape substantially decreases CRB while ensuring communication quality compared with existing rigid arrays.
tldr: This paper uses deep reinforcement learning to jointly optimize beamforming and surface shape of a flexible intelligent metasurface for integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems.
motivation: ISAC systems require high-precision sensing and reliable communication, but existing rigid arrays limit performance. Flexible intelligent metasurfaces offer adaptability, yet joint optimization of beamforming and surface shape is challenging.
method: The authors formulate a non-convex optimization problem minimizing the Cramér-Rao bound under QoS and power constraints, and solve it using a deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG) actor-critic DRL scheme with constraint-aware rewards.
result: Numerical results show that joint optimization significantly reduces the CRB while maintaining communication quality compared to rigid arrays.
conclusion: The proposed DRL-based approach effectively enhances sensing performance in FIM-aided ISAC systems, demonstrating the benefit of flexible metasurfaces.

title: A Contextual-Bandit Oversight Game With Two-Sided Informational Asymmetry
authors: Yunjin Tong
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00155v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study runtime human oversight of an AI agent when private information runs in both directions: the human privately knows her reward function, while the AI privately knows the quality of the action it proposes. This is the kind of asymmetry that arises naturally when an autonomous robot or software agent has inspected a situation its human supervisor cannot directly assess. Building on Cooperative Inverse Reinforcement Learning (CIRL) and the Oversight Game, we introduce a contextual-bandit team game with two-sided asymmetric information and a play/ask/trust/oversee interface. The bandit structure removes physical state transitions and thereby yields exact one-shot characterizations that would remain conjectural in the full POMDP setting, though the common belief remains a dynamically controlled state across rounds. We give two one-shot characterizations, a team optimum and a behaviorally natural myopic rule, whose gap is a slab of avoidable harm: a region in which the AI privately knows the proposed action is harmful and shutdown would help, yet a myopic human, trusting her prior, declines to oversee. We show this gap is the price of non-credible oversight communication, and give a partial analysis of how it resolves dynamically over repeated rounds through passive learning and active signaling with a one-period-lagged oversight response.
tldr: This paper studies a contextual-bandit oversight game with two-sided informational asymmetry between a human and an AI agent, focusing on the gap between team-optimal and myopic behavior.
motivation: To understand the challenges of runtime human oversight of AI agents when both the human's reward function and the AI's action quality are private information.
method: The paper models the interaction as a contextual-bandit team game with a play/ask/trust/oversee interface, providing one-shot characterizations of team optimum and a myopic rule.
result: It identifies a 'slab of avoidable harm' where the AI knows an action is harmful but a myopic human declines to oversee, and shows this gap is the price of non-credible oversight communication.
conclusion: The gap can be partially resolved over repeated rounds through passive learning and active signaling with a one-period-lagged oversight response.

title: From Signals To Structure: How Memory Architecture Drives Language Emergence In Llm Agents
authors: Yashar Talebirad, Eden Redman, Ali Parsaee, Osmar R. Zaiane
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00233v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: How do two agents invent a shared language from scratch? In a Lewis signaling game, a sender and receiver must coordinate on a code using only their interaction history. We study five memory architectures across varying channel configurations with LLM agents and find that memory architecture matters more than channel capacity. Agents with a persistent private notebook benefit from surplus channel capacity and avoid the high-capacity collapse seen in stateless agents, achieving the most reliable coordination ([MATH] at capacity = 25). Stateless agents peak at moderate capacity and then degrade as the vocabulary grows beyond what a rolling context window can track The notebook externalizes learned conventions, freeing agents from having to re-derive codes each round. An information bottleneck-inspired argument predicts an optimal capacity equal to the number of objects. Instead, the bottleneck (capacity = 8) proves to be a fragility point, and surplus capacity is generally better. We show that channel capacity alone cannot predict coordination; memory architecture determines whether agents turn interaction history into stable conventions, and both dimensions are needed to understand how signals become language.
tldr: This paper studies language emergence in LLM agents using Lewis signaling games, focusing on memory architecture and channel capacity.
motivation: Understanding how agents invent shared language from scratch is a fundamental question in AI and cognitive science, with implications for multi-agent communication.
method: Five memory architectures (including persistent notebook and stateless) are tested with LLM agents in signaling games across varying channel capacities.
result: Memory architecture, especially a persistent private notebook, significantly improves coordination and avoids high-capacity collapse, while stateless agents degrade at high capacities.
conclusion: Channel capacity alone cannot predict coordination; memory architecture determines whether interaction history becomes stable conventions.

title: A Scoping Review Of Physics Informed Machine Learning For Wave Propagation Modeling In Seismology
authors: \'oscar Rinc\'on-Carde\~no, Gregorio P\'erez-Bernal, Silvana Montoya-Noguera, Nicol\'as Guar\'in-Zapata
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00178v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standard numerical methods accurately simulate seismic waves but are computationally expensive, particularly for inverse problems. Machine learning approaches have been proposed as alternatives that can reduce computational cost while maintaining acceptable physical accuracy. To map how physics-informed machine learning methods have been applied to seismic wave propagation modeling based on partial differential equations. A scoping review was conducted using the OpenAlex and Scopus databases. Selected studies were classified by problem type (forward or inverse) and machine learning strategy to identify research trends, methodological patterns, and gaps in the literature. Physics-informed machine learning has been applied to both forward modeling and inversion in seismology, often reaching accuracy comparable to standard numerical methods at lower computational cost. Application of three mechanisms for incorporating physical knowledge were identified: observational bias, inductive bias, and learning bias. To evaluate methodological reproducibility of a representative method, the original PINN framework was replicated in PyTorch, obtaining results consistent with and in most cases more accurate than those originally reported. From the reviewed literature, limitations remain in benchmarking consistency, training cost, and scalability to three-dimensional and experimentally validated problems. Standard numerical methods remain the basis of seismological workflows, while physics-informed machine learning offers complementary approaches that are useful for inverse problems and surrogate modeling. Future work should focus on consistent benchmarking, hybrid formulations, and validation under realistic geophysical conditions.
tldr: A scoping review of physics-informed machine learning for seismic wave propagation modeling.
motivation: Standard numerical methods for seismic wave simulation are computationally expensive, especially for inverse problems; machine learning offers potential speedups.
method: The authors conducted a scoping review using OpenAlex and Scopus, classified studies by problem type and ML strategy, and replicated a representative PINN framework in PyTorch.
result: Physics-informed ML achieves comparable accuracy to numerical methods at lower cost; three mechanisms for incorporating physics were identified; reproducibility was confirmed.
conclusion: Physics-informed ML is a complementary approach for seismology, but limitations remain in benchmarking, training cost, and scalability; future work should focus on consistent benchmarking and hybrid methods.

title: X-ray Coherent Attosecond Pulse Pair Spectroscopy
authors: Zain Abhari, Thomas M. Linker, Thomas Kroll, Yurina Michine, Gota Yamaguchi, Yuichi Inubushi, Taito Osaka, Jumpei Yamada, Ichiro Inoue, Makina Yabashi, Aliaksei Halavanau, Andrei Benediktovitch, Nina Rohringer, Matthias F. Kling, Claudio Pelligrini, Hitoki Yoneda, Uwe Bergmann
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00285v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: X-ray free electron laser (XFEL) experiments using self-amplified spontaneous emission (SASE) pulses typically achieve temporal resolutions of order several femtoseconds, as the pulse duration puts a practical limit to pump-probe or probe-probe schemes. Even with the emerging capabilities to generate pulses with attosecond durations with new single-spike SASE schemes, direct access to attosecond electron dynamics remains an experimental challenge. Here we show how X-ray coherent attosecond pulse-pair spectroscopy (X-CAPPS) provides a powerful new approach to access the ultrashort time-delay window. Coherent attosecond pulse pairs with time delays varying from ~500 as to ~5 fs are generated with Cu K[MATH] stimulated X-ray emission from a gain medium pumped by intense SASE XFEL pulses. These pulse pairs are analyzed with two subsequent Bragg crystal spectrometers, and the resulting interference spectrum is captured on two sequential 2D image detectors encoding their time separation, relative amplitudes, and phases with high precision. X-CAPPS requires no split-and-delay X-ray optics, nor XFEL pulse modifications, making it broadly implementable across existing facilities. This technique enables the investigation of attosecond processes with [MATH]ngstr\"{o}m resolution, providing a new tool for probing ultrafast dynamics across a wide range of atomic, molecular, and solid systems.
tldr: This paper presents a new X-ray spectroscopy technique using coherent attosecond pulse pairs to achieve attosecond temporal resolution for probing ultrafast dynamics.
motivation: Current XFEL experiments are limited to femtosecond resolution, preventing direct access to attosecond electron dynamics. The authors aim to overcome this limitation with a novel spectroscopic method.
method: Coherent attosecond pulse pairs are generated via stimulated X-ray emission from a gain medium pumped by SASE XFEL pulses, and their interference spectrum is analyzed using Bragg crystal spectrometers and 2D detectors.
result: The technique enables time delays from ~500 as to ~5 fs with high precision, requiring no split-and-delay optics or XFEL modifications.
conclusion: X-CAPPS provides a broadly implementable tool for probing attosecond processes with angstrom resolution across atomic, molecular, and solid systems.

title: Wallis Products From The Four-Dimensional Singular Harmonic Oscillator
authors: Bin Ye, Ruitao Chen, Lei Yin
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00340v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a variational derivation of the Wallis product and its reciprocal from the four-dimensional singular harmonic oscillator. The inverse-square interaction is absorbed into an effective angular parameter [MATH], so that the lowest exact energy in a fixed sector is [MATH]. Motivated by the radial Kustaanheimo--Stiefel relation [MATH] between the four-dimensional oscillator and the three-dimensional Coulomb problem, we use the quartic trial family [MATH]. The minimized variational energy yields an accuracy ratio governed by adjacent Gamma functions. In the large-[MATH] semiclassical limit, this ratio approaches unity. Restricting [MATH] to the odd sequence [MATH] gives the standard Wallis product, whereas the even sequence [MATH] gives its reciprocal form. The Coulomb-dual interpretation further relates the two branches to integer and half-integer effective angular sectors in the dual Coulomb/MICZ description. The result shows that Wallis-type infinite products persist under an inverse-square deformation of the oscillator and arise from a common Gamma-function structure in radial variational dynamics.
tldr: This paper derives Wallis products from a four-dimensional singular harmonic oscillator using variational methods and the Kustaanheimo-Stiefel transformation.
motivation: To explore the connection between Wallis-type infinite products and quantum mechanical systems, specifically the four-dimensional harmonic oscillator with an inverse-square potential.
method: A variational approach with a quartic trial family is used, exploiting the radial Kustaanheimo-Stiefel relation to map the problem to the three-dimensional Coulomb problem.
result: The variational energy ratio yields adjacent Gamma functions; restricting to odd or even sequences gives the standard Wallis product or its reciprocal, respectively.
conclusion: Wallis-type products arise from a common Gamma-function structure in radial variational dynamics, persisting under inverse-square deformation of the oscillator.

title: Finite-Size Effect Induced Spatial-Spectral Mode Splitting In Membrane Metasurfaces
authors: Chih-Zong Deng, Mu-Hsin Chen, Chun-Hao Chiang, Jui-Han Fu, Vincent Tung, Masanobu Iwanaga, Ya-Lun Ho
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00468v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work reports the spatial-spectral engineering and finite-size quantization of optical modes within a triangular-lattice silicon nitride membrane metasurface. Truncating the lattice into a finite square cavity breaks translational symmetry and lifts modal degeneracy, splitting optical modes into discrete cavity-envelope sub-modes. High-resolution photoluminescence (PL) scanning reveals distinct spatial field distributions. The corner-localized sub-mode features the highest Q-factor due to multipolar far-field destructive interference, whereas the core-localized sub-mode exhibits strong radiative coupling. PL mapping reveals a symmetric, four-fold clover-like wavelength arrangement. These results demonstrate that boundary-induced deterministic symmetry can override underlying lattice characteristics, offering a robust strategy for precise spatial-spectral tailoring of light-matter interactions at the nanoscale.
tldr: This paper studies spatial-spectral mode splitting in a membrane metasurface due to finite-size effects, focusing on nanophotonic engineering rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To understand how boundary-induced symmetry breaking can tailor light-matter interactions at the nanoscale for applications in nanophotonics.
method: Experimental photoluminescence scanning and numerical simulations of a triangular-lattice silicon nitride membrane metasurface truncated into a finite square cavity.
result: Discrete cavity-envelope sub-modes with distinct spatial field distributions and Q-factors are observed, including corner-localized and core-localized modes.
conclusion: Finite-size quantization provides a robust strategy for precise spatial-spectral control of optical modes in metasurfaces.

title: Evanescent Absorption Spectroscopy Of Transition Metal Dichalcogenide Materials Using Guided Photoluminescence In Si$_3$N$_4$ Photonic Waveguides
authors: Victor Gonzalez-Morote (mind-In2ub, University Of Barcelona, Barcelona, Spain), Marianna Sledzinska (catalan Institute Of Nanoscience And Nanotechnology), Arkadiusz P. Gertych (faculty Of Physics, Warsaw University Of Technology, Warsaw, Poland), Syed Hassan Abbas Jaffery (faculty Of Physics, Warsaw University Of Technology, Warsaw, Poland), Mariusz Zdrojek (faculty Of Physics, Warsaw University Of Technology, Warsaw, Poland), Daniel Navarro-Urrios
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-chip integration of two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) with photonic waveguides underpins a growing class of compact optoelectronic and sensing devices, whose performance depends on the optical absorption of the 2D material in this integrated environment. We demonstrate source-free, on-chip evanescent absorption spectroscopy of MoS[MATH] and WS[MATH] flakes integrated on Si[MATH]N[MATH] waveguides, in which the broadband defect-related photoluminescence of the Si[MATH]N[MATH] core itself acts as the internal probe. Light generated inside the core propagates under the TMD flake and is spectrally attenuated by evanescent interaction with the 2D material, and normalizing the transmitted spectrum to a reference waveguide without TMD yields the energy-dependent absorption response without any external illumination. The extracted guided absorption agrees with Raman and local micro-photoluminescence characterization and resolves differences between spatially uniform and non-uniform flakes. A complementary top-pumping scheme recovers guided WS[MATH] photoluminescence, whose spectral reshaping during propagation is quantitatively reproduced by the measured absorption. This source-free platform qualifies 2D materials in their integrated photonic environment and provides a direct route toward waveguide-integrated TMD photodetectors and sensors.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a source-free evanescent absorption spectroscopy technique for TMD materials using guided photoluminescence in Si3N4 waveguides.
motivation: On-chip integration of TMDs with photonic waveguides requires characterization of optical absorption in the integrated environment, but conventional methods rely on external illumination.
method: The authors use the broadband defect-related photoluminescence of the Si3N4 waveguide core as an internal probe; light propagates under the TMD flake and is spectrally attenuated by evanescent interaction, and normalization to a reference waveguide yields the absorption spectrum.
result: The extracted guided absorption agrees with Raman and micro-photoluminescence characterization and resolves differences between uniform and non-uniform flakes; a complementary top-pumping scheme recovers guided WS2 photoluminescence whose spectral reshaping is reproduced by the measured absorption.
conclusion: This source-free platform qualifies 2D materials in their integrated photonic environment and provides a direct route toward waveguide-integrated TMD photodetectors and sensors.

title: Implementation Filters And Delay-Budget Instability In Coupled Replicator--Mutator Dynamics
authors: Alexander Omelchenko
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00227v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We model an adaptive contest in which two antagonistically coupled populations continually reallocate effort among competing methods, but decisions are not fielded instantly. Each side has an intended portfolio and a deployed portfolio: intended reallocations follow delayed observations of the opponent, while deployment follows intent through a first-order implementation filter. Under barycentric balance and uniform exploration, the linearized scalar branches have a characteristic factor in which hard observation and deployment lags enter only through their total sum, whereas implementation rates enter through real filter factors that cannot be absorbed into selection or exploration. In the strictly antagonistic class, negative spectral branches split into three regimes: weak branches have no positive-frequency crossing, intermediate branches lose stability through a delay-induced Hopf bifurcation, and strong branches are at or beyond the implementation-filter instability margin already at zero hard delay. This gives an operational delay-budget rule: in the delay-induced window, reducing any hard lag has the same first-order stabilizing leverage at onset; in the filter-induced regime, hard-lag reduction alone cannot restore stability. Balanced scalar performance observables generically show a mean shift and a second harmonic at twice the compositional frequency, and under strict antagonism the two performance signals are locked in antiphase with fixed amplitude ratio. For a baseline branch, a finite-dimensional Hopf normal-form calculation gives a negative cubic coefficient, and direct simulations reproduce the predicted threshold, amplitude scaling, and observable signatures. Motivating applications include cybersecurity and rapid technological countermeasure adaptation.
tldr: This paper models an adaptive contest between two populations with delayed observations and implementation filters, analyzing stability regimes and delay-budget rules.
motivation: To understand how delays and implementation filters affect the stability and performance of coupled replicator-mutator dynamics in adversarial settings.
method: The authors use linearized scalar branches, Hopf bifurcation analysis, and normal-form calculations to study stability regimes and performance observables.
result: They identify three stability regimes (weak, intermediate, strong) and derive a delay-budget rule: in the delay-induced window, reducing any hard lag has equal stabilizing leverage, while in the filter-induced regime, hard-lag reduction alone cannot restore stability.
conclusion: The findings provide operational rules for managing delays in adaptive contests, with applications to cybersecurity and technological countermeasure adaptation.

title: Structural Visibility In Dynamical Systems On Hypergraphs: A Pattern Formation Perspective
authors: Anthony M. Bloch Moise R. Mouyebe
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00256v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hypergraphs encode rich multiway interactions, but not all structural information is equally accessible through the dynamics. By analyzing pattern-forming instabilities in reaction-diffusion systems on directed hypergraphs, this work develops a theory of structural visibility that characterizes which features of higher-order structure survive successive levels of dynamical reduction. It is established that higher-order structure is not automatically dynamically relevant. Linearization destroys most higher-order information. Meanwhile, nonlinear reduction recovers only specific higher-order marginals of the adjacency tensor, and projection along critical directions further filters what is dynamically visible. First, we show that the linearized dynamics depends on the hypergraph only through its first-tail-moment statistics, termed exposure. Consequently, exposure-equivalent hypergraphs are linearly indistinguishable in the sense that they exhibit identical dispersion relations and instability thresholds. Next, we define a hierarchy of hyperedge tail-moments that captures progressively detailed co-occurence, and we prove a structural decomposition theorem describing how contractions of these tensors, termed packing effects, influence the reduced amplitude dynamics. This leads to a visibility hierarchy in which successive asymptotic orders reveal increasingly richer structural information. More specifically, exposure governs linear onset while packing effects control post-onset dynamics. Finally, we establish results on nonlinear distinguishability, characterizing when linearly indistinguishable higher-order systems may exhibit different post-onset behaviors. In addition, we formalize when higher-order systems become dynamically indistinguishable from pairwise systems, leading to the notion of dynamical graph surrogacy. Numerical simulations support the theoretical predictions.
tldr: This paper studies structural visibility in reaction-diffusion systems on directed hypergraphs, focusing on pattern formation and dynamical reduction.
motivation: To understand which features of higher-order hypergraph structure are dynamically relevant in pattern-forming systems.
method: Analyzes linear and nonlinear dynamics of reaction-diffusion systems on directed hypergraphs, introducing exposure and packing effects to characterize structural visibility.
result: Linearized dynamics depends only on first-tail-moment statistics (exposure); nonlinear reduction recovers higher-order marginals; a visibility hierarchy emerges where successive orders reveal more structural information.
conclusion: Higher-order structure is not automatically dynamically relevant; linearization destroys most higher-order information, but nonlinear dynamics can recover some, leading to conditions for dynamical graph surrogacy.

title: Rigorous Analysis Of The Time-splitting Methods For The Semiclassical Dirac Equation
authors: Jia Yin He Wang

method: The authors analyze first-order, second-order, and fourth-order compact time-splitting schemes, proving mass preservation and deriving error estimates that depend on time step, spatial mesh size, and the Planck constant.

title: Performance Evaluation Of A Certain Transceiver Architecture For Multiple-Input Multiple-Output Phase-Modulated Channels
authors: Hengyu Cui, Ru-Han Chen, Zhenyao He, Shijun Zhu, Ruoqi Sun, Yeqin Tai
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00356v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) channels with phase modulation, we recently proposed a method of unitarily transforming the channel matrix into a certain row-echelon form, by which the original MIMO channel can be converted into a certain number of scalar sub-channels with two phase inputs, thereby forming an annulus constellation geometry, and corrupted by both the additive white Gaussian noise and weak self-interference. In this paper, several bounds are derived to evaluate the fundamental limit of such a specific transceiver architecture. Two upper bounds are obtained by upper-bounding the capacity of a scalar channel with an annulus support constraint from the perspective of the convex geometry, while a lower bound is obtained by the standard entropy power inequality. Numerical results show that the gaps between these bounds are small at high signal-to-noise ratios for the MIMO phase-modulated channels over the Rayleigh fading and the single-input multiple-output symbiotic communication system assisted by a reconfigurable intelligent surface.
tldr: This paper evaluates a transceiver architecture for MIMO phase-modulated channels using convex geometry and entropy power inequality.
motivation: To derive bounds on the capacity of a specific MIMO transceiver architecture with phase modulation.
method: Upper bounds via convex geometry and lower bound via entropy power inequality.
result: Gaps between bounds are small at high SNR for Rayleigh fading and RIS-assisted SIMO systems.
conclusion: The proposed architecture shows promise for MIMO phase-modulated channels.

title: Effective Dynamics Of The Sinkhorn Algorithm In The Regime Of Low Entropy Regularization
authors: Guillaume Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00665v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Sinkhorn algorithm is the de facto standard method for numerically solving entropy-regularized optimal transport problems over finite sets. In this work, we investigate a phenomenon arising when Sinkhorn is applied with a small regularization parameter [MATH]: the evolution of the dual variables (the logarithm of the scaling factors) is approximately piecewise-linear, while the primal variables (the approximate transport plans) exhibit a saddle-to-saddle type behavior. We prove that as [MATH], the Sinkhorn iterates indeed converge to a continuous-time curve consistent with these observations, when time is rescaled as [MATH], and we characterize the limiting "cold Sinkhorn" dynamics explicitly. In particular, we show that it acts as a dual optimization dynamics for the unregularized problem with properties analogous to the simplex algorithm. Notably, this dynamics converges in finite time to an unregularized solution, implying a novel guarantee for the Sinkhorn algorithm itself: it achieves [MATH] dual suboptimality in [MATH] iterations, instead of [MATH] as existing analyses would suggest.
tldr: This paper analyzes the dynamics of the Sinkhorn algorithm for entropy-regularized optimal transport in the low-regularization regime, showing convergence to a piecewise-linear curve and finite-time convergence to an unregularized solution.
motivation: The Sinkhorn algorithm is widely used for optimal transport, but its behavior under small regularization is not well understood. The authors aim to characterize the dynamics and prove convergence guarantees.
method: The authors study the continuous-time limit of the Sinkhorn iterations as the regularization parameter goes to zero, rescaling time appropriately, and derive explicit limiting dynamics.
result: They prove that the iterates converge to a continuous-time curve with piecewise-linear dual variables and saddle-to-saddle primal behavior, and that the limiting dynamics converges in finite time to an unregularized solution, implying an improved iteration complexity bound.
conclusion: The work provides a novel theoretical understanding of the Sinkhorn algorithm in the low-regularization regime, with implications for optimal transport computation.

title: Bayesian Updates From Coalgebraic Determinisation
authors: Nathaniel Virgo Manuel Baltieri
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The powerset construction is the classical determinisation procedure for nondeterministic finite automata. In the coalgebraic setting, this construction has been generalised to structured coalgebras, which are coalgebras equipped with extra data. For stochastic Moore machines over the distribution monad, a type of structured coalgebra, the determinisation construction induces a semantics assigning to each finite input word a distribution on the current output. This semantics is appropriate when only the current output matters, but it is too coarse for settings in which intermediate observations must also be taken into account, as is typical for agents solving POMDPs in control theory and reinforcement learning. In these contexts, agents need to condition on all realised observations, not just the final one, so to better plan for the future. This has been addressed from a category theoretic perspective through a procedure called ``unifilarisation'', which (in our context) takes a stochastic Mealy machine and produces a machine whose states are priors over the original state space and whose transitions are given by Bayesian filtering. Here we show that unifilarisation is an instance of coalgebraic determinisation. We work with Mealy machines over monads equipped with extra structure generalising the notion of the support of a distribution. We show that in this setting, unifilarisation arises from the general determinisation procedure. We then compare the resulting final coalgebra semantics with the Moore-style one. Instead of assigning only a distribution on current outputs to each finite input word, it yields causal stochastic behaviours, that is, families mapping input words to distributions on output words compatible with the ``causality'' constraint that outputs cannot depend on future inputs.
tldr: The paper presents a coalgebraic framework for unifilarisation of stochastic Mealy machines, showing it as an instance of determinisation.
motivation: To provide a categorical semantics for agents that condition on all observations, as needed in control theory and reinforcement learning, which is not captured by Moore-style semantics.
method: The authors work with Mealy machines over monads with extra structure generalising support of a distribution, and show that unifilarisation arises from the general coalgebraic determinisation procedure.
result: Unifilarisation yields causal stochastic behaviours, mapping input words to distributions on output words respecting causality, rather than just distributions on current outputs.
conclusion: The coalgebraic perspective unifies determinisation and unifilarisation, offering a principled semantics for sequential decision-making under uncertainty.

title: Scalable Security And Migration-Aware Sfc Provisioning In Leo Satellite Networks
authors: Mohammed Mahyoub, Wael Jaafar, Sami Muhaidat, Halim Yanikomeroglu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00471v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite constellations are emerging as a backbone for global 6G connectivity, where independent tenant slices share orbital infrastructure, each requiring an ordered chain of security virtual network functions (VNFs). Because onboard computation and networking are scarce, slices cannot be given dedicated VNFs. They must share instances on the same satellites, enlarging the attack surface and exposing tenants to cross-slice side-channel risk. This exposure shifts continually as visibility, orbital motion, and the inter-satellite topology change in time (epochs), making VNF migration a structural necessity that couples resource efficiency, service continuity, and security isolation into a single problem. We formulate this security- and migration-aware security function chain (SFC) placement as a multi-slice mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) whose core is a co-location risk model, grounded in ISO/NIST principles and supported by analytic bounds, in which we separate avoidable migrations from those forced by orbital motion. Because the joint program scales quadratically with the cross-slice co-location terms, we develop an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM)-inspired penalized per-slice best response decomposition that recasts the coupling as a linear per-slice penalty, yielding independent subproblems through sequential (S-ADMM) and parallel, collision-repaired (P-ADMM) schedules. Simulations over a Walker-Delta satellite constellation show that the proposed framework eliminates co-location risk, reduces SFC migrations, and sustains full delay compliance, while remaining feasible within the per-epoch budget for slice counts where the monolithic security-aware MILP is intractable.
