tldr: This paper studies fair allocation of graph vertices under conflict constraints using strong colorability, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The problem of fair allocation under conflict constraints is a combinatorial optimization problem in graph theory and algorithmic fairness.
method: The paper introduces a hierarchy of variants of the strong chromatic number and uses it to derive existential and algorithmic results for fairness criteria like SD-EF1, EF1, and EF[1,1].
result: The authors characterize the number of agents needed for SD-EF1 allocations and provide sufficient conditions for EF1 and EF[1,1], with polynomial-time algorithms for graphs with bounded maximum degree.
conclusion: The work establishes a connection between fair allocation and strong colorability, but it is unrelated to quantum information theory or thermodynamics.

title: Antaeus: Hunting Repository-Level Logic Vulnerabilities Via Context-Grounded Llm Reasoning
authors: Michele Armillotta, Nicol\`o Romandini, Rebecca Montanari, Lorenzo Cavallaro
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based vulnerability detectors have shown promising results in identifying memory-safety bugs and vulnerability classes whose violations can often be expressed through established security properties. Logic vulnerabilities, however, pose a different challenge, as their identification requires inferring application-specific security invariants and implicit assumptions about intended behavior. Even frontier agentic models struggle because these invariants are often implicit and buried among unrelated code. Motivated by this gap, we present Antaeus, a framework for detecting logic vulnerabilities that grounds LLM reasoning in repository-level code context. Antaeus follows a repository-scale pipeline combining function prioritization, context-grounded reasoning, comparative validation, and structured reporting. It ranks functions using lightweight repo-wide security signals, directing costly LLM analysis toward relevant code and reducing calls, cost, and triage effort. For each prioritized function, Antaeus combines local code context with a repository-level view of the application's functionality, security resources, and trust boundaries. This enables reasoning about how the function is executed within the broader application rather than as an isolated snippet. Antaeus identifies security-sensitive sinks, derives safety conditions for safe execution, and checks whether they are locally satisfied. Candidate findings undergo comparative validation, pruning concerns that reflect project-wide norms rather than distinctive violations. Finally, Antaeus reports sinks, violated safety conditions, and evidence, making findings actionable and traceable. We evaluate Antaeus on 28 repositories with confirmed logic vulnerabilities and compare it against function-level and agentic models. Antaeus detects and explains 15 vulnerabilities, outperforming baselines with comparable token usage and cost.
tldr: Antaeus is a framework for detecting logic vulnerabilities in software repositories using LLM reasoning grounded in repository-level context.
motivation: Logic vulnerabilities are hard to detect because they require understanding application-specific security invariants and implicit assumptions, which current LLM-based detectors struggle with.
method: Antaeus prioritizes functions using lightweight security signals, then applies context-grounded LLM reasoning with repository-level views to identify safety conditions and validate findings through comparative validation.
result: On 28 repositories with confirmed logic vulnerabilities, Antaeus detected and explained 15 vulnerabilities, outperforming function-level and agentic baselines with comparable token usage.
conclusion: Antaeus demonstrates that grounding LLM reasoning in repository-level context improves detection of logic vulnerabilities, making findings actionable and traceable.

title: Online Fair Division Meets Reordering Buffers
authors: Georgios Amanatidis, Giulio Giaconi, Evangelos Markakis, Nicos Protopapas
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01159v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the online fair division of indivisible mixed manna among agents with additive valuation functions. Under the standard online model, at each time step an indivisible item arrives; each agent may assign it a positive, negative, or zero value, and it must be irrevocably allocated, before the arrival of the next item. At the same time, we also wish to maintain some fairness guarantee, and in this work we focus on envy-freeness (EF) and one of its most prominent relaxations, envy-freeness up to one item (EF1). Given the strong negative and the scarce positive results for this problem without additional assumptions, we augment our algorithms with buffers that can store and rearrange a limited number of items. This setting interpolates naturally between the fully online case (no buffer) and the fully offline case (a buffer large enough to hold all items). We show that algorithms equipped with reasonably sized buffers can achieve strong guarantees for personalized [MATH]-value instances, i.e., instances in which each agent assigns at most [MATH] distinct values to items. In particular, we construct allocations that are EF1 at every time step and EF at most time steps, using a buffer of size linear in [MATH] and in the number of agents. Our approach relies on novel combinatorial arguments and on constructing a sequence of envy-free matchings that allocates most items. Finally, we extend our results to general additive valuation functions, with a dependence on the largest per-agent ratio between two values of the same sign, and we also identify limitations of our approach via impossibility results on the use of buffers with smaller size.
tldr: This paper studies online fair division of mixed manna with buffers to achieve envy-freeness guarantees.
motivation: Online fair division without additional assumptions has strong negative results; buffers provide a natural interpolation between online and offline settings.
method: Algorithms with buffers of size linear in the number of distinct values and agents are designed, using combinatorial arguments and a sequence of envy-free matchings.
result: EF1 at every time step and EF at most time steps are achieved for personalized value instances; results extend to general additive valuations with limitations.
conclusion: Buffers enable strong fairness guarantees in online fair division, but impossibility results show buffer size requirements are tight.

title: Detecting Adversarial Evasion Attacks Against Autoencoder-Based Network Intrusion Detection Systems
authors: Ashim Siwakoti Niklas Bunzel
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01194v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evasion attacks deliberately manipulate input to an ML-based system to produce an incorrect prediction while the manipulated input still appears benign. The PANDA framework has demonstrated that adversarial examples developed for the vision domain can be transferred to the network domain by converting packet sequences into invertible grayscale images, enabling gradient-based attacks such as masked FGSM against autoencoder-based network intrusion detection systems (NIDS). These attacks manipulate the NIDS anomaly score without altering the underlying attack semantics, leaving defenders without a straightforward way to distinguish between benign flows and carefully perturbed malicious traffic. In this paper, we propose two complementary detectors: the Residual Localisation Detector (RLD), which tracks the spatial concentration of reconstruction errors in the inter-arrival time feature region in image space; and the Feature-Space Perturbation Consistency (FPC) Detector, which operates directly on packet-level inter-arrival time features in packet-feature space. We evaluate both detectors on benign, malicious, and adversarial traffic from multiple IoT devices in the UQ-IoT dataset. Both detectors achieve near-perfect detection performance (TNR, TPR, precision, recall, and F1-score [MATH]) against adversarial examples across the evaluated IoT traffic. Our results indicate that integrating reconstruction-based scoring with perturbation consistency checks, in both image space and packet-feature space, offers a practical defence against emerging PANDA-style adversarial attacks on NIDS.
tldr: This paper proposes detectors for adversarial evasion attacks against autoencoder-based network intrusion detection systems, focusing on IoT network security.
motivation: Adversarial evasion attacks can manipulate NIDS anomaly scores without altering attack semantics, making detection challenging. The authors aim to develop practical defenses against such attacks.
method: Two detectors are proposed: Residual Localisation Detector (RLD) tracks spatial concentration of reconstruction errors in image space, and Feature-Space Perturbation Consistency (FPC) Detector operates on packet-level features. Both are evaluated on benign, malicious, and adversarial traffic from IoT devices.
result: Both detectors achieve near-perfect detection performance (TNR, TPR, precision, recall, F1-score) against adversarial examples across evaluated IoT traffic.
conclusion: Integrating reconstruction-based scoring with perturbation consistency checks offers a practical defense against PANDA-style adversarial attacks on NIDS.

title: All-out Attack: Optimal Block Withholding Under Pay-Per-Share Scheme
authors: Sennur Ulukus Mustafa Doger
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01209v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical Block Withholding (BWH) attacks have been extensively studied in block-dependent reward schemes, where pool members are compensated upon a block discovery within the pool. However, most contemporary mining pools operate under share-based scheme wherein participants are paid immediately upon submission of valid shares. In this paper, we analyze BWH under Pay-Per-Share (PPS) and Full-PPS (FPPS) schemes for Nakamoto-style blockchains and prove that these mechanisms are not incentive compatible -- contrary to claims in prior literature. Under PPS/FPPS, the optimal strategy for a BWH attacker is the All-out Attack (AoA): the adversary allocates its entire hashpower toward the victim pool, submitting only partial Proof-of-Work shares (pPoW) while withholding all valid blocks, i.e., full Proof-of-Work (fPoW). Under AoA, prior to the first difficulty adjustment, the adversary incurs negligible loss due to the withheld fPoWs. After the first difficulty adjustment, which reduces block difficulty, the adversary generates more pPoWs per unit time, achieving a relative gain of [MATH] compared to pre-adjustment rates, where [MATH] is the fraction of adversarial hashpower. Moreover, per unit time and per unit hashpower, all honest miners benefit at the same rate as the adversary. In contrast, the victim pool operator incurs losses: it pays the attacker out-of-pocket for pPoW submissions but receives no fPoW compensation in return. Finally, advanced variants of BWH, such as Fork After Withholding (FAW), do not yield additional profit to the attacker.
tldr: This paper analyzes block withholding attacks in Bitcoin mining under Pay-Per-Share reward schemes, proving they are not incentive compatible and proposing an optimal attack strategy.
motivation: Classical block withholding attacks were studied for block-dependent rewards, but most modern pools use share-based schemes like PPS/FPPS, whose incentive compatibility was previously claimed but not rigorously analyzed.
method: The authors model the Pay-Per-Share and Full-PPS reward mechanisms mathematically and derive the optimal adversarial strategy (All-out Attack) by comparing attacker gains before and after difficulty adjustments.
result: Under PPS/FPPS, the optimal attack is to allocate all hashpower to the victim pool, submitting partial proofs-of-work but withholding full blocks, leading to relative gains for the attacker after difficulty adjustment and losses for the pool operator.
conclusion: PPS/FPPS schemes are not incentive compatible; the All-out Attack is optimal and more profitable than advanced variants like Fork After Withholding.

title: Towards An Automated AI-based Framework For Floor Plan Compliance Checks For Residential Buildings
authors: Subash Gautam, Debaditya Acharya, Alexandra Kleeman, Sarah Foster
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00015v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: To improve residents' well-being in Australia's urban areas, governments have introduced policy reforms such as SEPP65, BADS, and SPP7.3 to enhance apartment design quality. These regulations require precise geometric and spatial analysis to evaluate health-related features, including daylight access, natural ventilation, privacy, and space efficiency. However, compliance checking remains challenging due to its manual, time-intensive nature. Additionally, evolving policies limit scalability for large-scale assessments across thousands of apartments. Existing automated floor plan analysis methods are fragmented and typically focus on single apartments, lacking a unified framework for multi-unit compliance checking. This article explores current advancements in automated floor plan analysis, particularly AI-driven approaches, and highlights key challenges in their practical adoption. To address these gaps, a conceptual framework is proposed for automated compliance checking in multi-apartment buildings. A Large Language Model (LLM) is used within a Rule Engine to convert textual building codes into executable, explainable rules. A Data Extraction Engine segments floor plan images into elements such as walls, rooms, fixtures, text, and symbols, and transforms them into a structured building graph with topological relationships. This structured representation is then evaluated by a Compliance Check Engine, which leverages LLM-generated rules for assessment. The proposed framework offers a scalable, consistent, and transparent approach to automated compliance checking across jurisdictions, supporting efficient enforcement of apartment design standards and promoting healthier, higher-density urban development.
tldr: This paper proposes an AI-based framework for automated compliance checking of residential building floor plans against Australian design regulations.
motivation: Manual compliance checking of floor plans is time-consuming and not scalable, especially for multi-unit buildings with evolving policies.
method: The framework uses a Large Language Model within a Rule Engine to convert building codes into executable rules, a Data Extraction Engine to segment floor plans into a structured building graph, and a Compliance Check Engine to evaluate the graph against the rules.
result: The paper presents a conceptual framework and discusses challenges, but does not provide experimental results or a working prototype.
conclusion: The proposed framework aims to provide a scalable, consistent, and transparent approach to automated compliance checking, but remains at the conceptual stage.

title: Determining The Complexity Of Chromatic Sum In Classes Defined By A Set Of Forbidden Graphs
authors: Cl\'ement Dallard, Dani\"el Paulusma, Erik Jan van Leeuwen
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00263v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Chromatic Sum problem asks, given a graph [MATH] and an integer [MATH], whether [MATH] admits a colouring [MATH] with sum [MATH]. We study the complexity of Chromatic Sum on graph classes defined by some set of forbidden graphs. First, we show that three known frameworks fully classify the complexity of Chromatic Sum on [MATH]-minor-free graphs and [MATH]-topological-minor-free graphs for any set of graphs [MATH], and on [MATH]-subgraph-free graphs for any finite set of graphs [MATH]. To show this, we prove a new NP-completeness result for Chromatic Sum on certain subdivisions of planar subcubic graphs. Next, we consider other containment relations. We formalise a novel framework of problems that are NP-complete for planar graphs as well as for graphs of bounded independence number. For every problem in this framework, we obtain an almost complete complexity classification on [MATH]-induced-minor-free graphs, [MATH]-induced-topological-minor-free graphs, and [MATH]-free graphs for every graph [MATH]. We show that Chromatic Sum belongs to this framework, as do several other problems. We also define a more fine-grained framework for the induced subgraph relation. We apply this to obtain a complete complexity classification for Chromatic Sum on [MATH]-free graphs, as well as for several other problems. We justify the choice of this framework by proving that Chromatic Sum is NP-complete for graphs of clique-width at most [MATH]. This result complements a known polynomial-time result for graphs of clique-width at most [MATH].
tldr: This paper studies the computational complexity of the Chromatic Sum problem on graph classes defined by forbidden subgraphs, minors, and induced subgraphs.
motivation: Understanding the complexity of graph coloring problems on restricted graph classes is a fundamental question in graph theory and algorithms.
method: The authors use known frameworks for classifying complexity on minor-free and subgraph-free graphs, and develop new frameworks for induced-minor-free and induced-topological-minor-free graphs, proving NP-completeness results via reductions from planar graph problems.
result: They provide full complexity classifications for Chromatic Sum on several graph classes defined by forbidden structures, and show NP-completeness for graphs of clique-width at most 3.
conclusion: The complexity of Chromatic Sum is now well-understood for many natural graph classes, with dichotomies between polynomial-time solvable and NP-complete cases.

title: Fast Deterministic Normal Bases And Circulant Polynomial Determinants
authors: Mark Giesbrecht, Armin Jamshidpey, \'eric Schost
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00313v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Let [MATH] be an algebraic extension of degree [MATH] over the finite field [MATH], given by a [MATH] monic and irreducible. It is classical that any such [MATH] contains an element [MATH] that is normal over [MATH], i.e., the conjugates [MATH] form an [MATH]-basis of [MATH]. In this paper we give a deterministic algorithm which finds such a normal element using [MATH] bit operations, for any [MATH]. The algorithm works by showing that, for a parameter [MATH], the element [MATH] is normal except for at most [MATH] values of [MATH]. This is established by constructing a "cleared Moore" circulant matrix over [MATH], whose determinant degree at most [MATH], such that [MATH] is normal if and only the determinant is non-zero at [MATH]. For faster computation over the base field, we replace this by an equivalent trace Gram circulant matrix over [MATH]. A main algorithmic contribution is a fast determinant algorithm for circulant matrices of polynomials, which uses triangular set projection and modular composition techniques to achieve a near-linear cost. Given an [MATH] circulant matrix over [MATH] whose entries have degree at most [MATH], we show how to compute its determinant deterministically with [MATH] bit operations. We complete the solution by showing how to extend this to finite fields of size less than [MATH], through an embedding in a low-degree extension field, at poly-logarithmic additional cost.
tldr: This paper presents a deterministic algorithm for finding normal bases in finite field extensions using circulant matrix determinant computation.
motivation: Normal bases are important for efficient arithmetic in finite fields, but deterministic algorithms for finding them have been inefficient.
method: The authors construct a cleared Moore circulant matrix and a trace Gram circulant matrix, then develop a fast determinant algorithm for circulant polynomial matrices using triangular set projection and modular composition.
result: The algorithm finds a normal element in O~(n^2 log q) bit operations for any finite field extension, and computes the circulant determinant in O~(n^2 d) bit operations.
conclusion: This work provides a practical deterministic method for normal basis construction, improving over previous probabilistic or less efficient approaches.
